title: Mental factors
hook: fifty-two factors that color each moment of consciousness

segments.voice: Yesterday, four families of mind: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant and functional. Your line: four families. When something unwelcome landed, could you call it a result, arriving? Day one thousand seventy-two.

A white shirt goes into the wash with one red sock and comes out pink. Same water. Same shirt. One small thing in the load, and everything has a new color. The Abhidhamma looks at a moment of mind in a similar way. In every moment there is a knowing, the plain fact of being aware of something. And riding along with that knowing are other things that tint it: interest, worry, kindness, hurry, ease. Today we meet the things that ride along.
screen: `ONE RED SOCK.` → `A KNOWING.` → `AND WHAT TINTS IT.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is cetasika, a mental factor. In the last days we met citta, consciousness, the bare knowing that arises and passes moment by moment. A citta never comes alone. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha, a manual of the Abhidhamma, describes a mental factor this way: it arises together with consciousness, ceases together with it, takes the same object, and rests on the same base. Partners, then, not visitors who wander in on their own schedule. The same manual counts fifty-two of them. The number matters less than the picture. One moment of seeing a friend's face is not only seeing. It is seeing plus recognition, plus warmth, plus maybe a small reminder that a call is overdue. The seeing is the citta. What flavors it is cetasika. The suttas have their own picture for this. In the Simile of the Cloth, the Buddha describes a cloth that is stained and dirty. Dip it in any dye, blue or yellow or red, and the color takes badly. Dip a clean cloth, and the color comes out clear. In the same way, he says, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected, and when it is clean, a happy one. The stains he names there include greed, ill will, anger, envy and conceit. The Abhidhamma takes lists like that and sorts them carefully: which factors stain, which brighten, and which are present no matter what. Here is why that is useful on an ordinary day. A mood, in this way of seeing, is a factor in a moment, one dye among several. It arrived, and it can pass. The knowing goes on knowing. What colors it keeps changing. Over the next days we meet the factors in families: the ones in every moment, the troubled ones, and the beautiful ones.
screen: `A CITTA NEVER COMES ALONE.` · `PARTNERS, NOT VISITORS.` · `A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.` · then, large: `A MOOD IS A FACTOR IN A MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then look at this moment the way a dyer looks at cloth. There is knowing: a sound, the feel of the seat, the breath. Now ask what color it has right now. Is there interest? Tiredness? A bit of hurry? Some ease? Name three, quietly, in plain words, like tired, curious, a little restless. Don't fix any of them. Just notice that each one is a color on the knowing, not the knowing itself. If the colors change while you sit, name the new ones. The bell holds the time.
Cetasika. A mental factor: something that arises with each moment of consciousness and colors it. Today's word.
Your line: what colors the mind. Today, when a mood shows up, try naming it as a factor instead of as yourself: impatience is here, rather than I'm impatient. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the mental factors as named lists, often from the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, and some meditation teachers use the same names to help students note what is present in the mind.

fork.setup: you're a dyer with a pot of good blue dye and a cloth that is stained and dirty. what do you do?
options: dip it straight in; the dye will cover the stains.
clean the cloth first, then dye it.
use a darker dye to hide the stains.
fork.reveal: in the Simile of the Cloth, a stained cloth takes any dye badly and a clean one takes it clear. the Buddha says the mind works the same way.

original.note: Pali cetasika: a mental factor, arising and ceasing together with consciousness.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mind is one thing.
what it means: each moment is a knowing plus the factors that color it.
what a scholar hears: the Abhidhammattha Sangaha defines a cetasika by four marks: it arises with consciousness, ceases with it, shares its object and shares its base.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (definition and count of the mental factors)
Majjhima Nikaya 7 (Vatthupama Sutta, the Simile of the Cloth)

notes: The four marks of a cetasika (arising together, ceasing together, same object, same base) and the count of fifty-two are from Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2 (cf. Shwe Zan Aung and C. A. F. Rhys Davids, Compendium of Philosophy, 1910). Confirm the plain-English wording.
MN 7 paraphrased: the dye colors (blue, yellow, red, carmine) and the list of defilements are summarized; 'an unhappy destination can be expected' paraphrases the sutta's conclusion. Confirm.
Checked against days 1062–1071: day 1066 used a stained-glass image for cetasika; this day uses cloth and dye (MN 7) instead.
The hook (shirt and red sock) is an everyday image, not a tradition claim.
Pronunciation in games.original is approximate; Pali stress varies by community.
